extracted.intended_audience: math-competition enthusiasts, problem-solvers, and researchers interested in AI theorem-proving
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how an LLM (o3-mini-high) performs on USAMO proof problems and what constitutes a valid, high-scoring USAMO proof; includes practical prompts and diagnostics for coaxing valid proofs from the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: USAMO scoring scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Each solution is scored on a 0–7 scale, with partial credit given sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percent scores shown are out of 7 (e.g. 1/7 = 14%). Two human experts grade each solution using a predefined rubric; averages across graders and runs are reported. This implies high standards for completeness and correctness — small omissions can lead to very low scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness / rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions to problems take the form of rigorous proofs, which are graded by human experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof must be logically correct; incorrect proofs can be superficially similar to correct ones and fail for a single misstated or omitted detail. There is no easy automatic test for natural-language proofs, so graders look for sound logical steps and valid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of premises (genre convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should use each premise or else mention if a premise is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to use an explicitly-stated hypothesis (e.g., 'n is odd') is a genre violation — it may indicate the proof is wrong or incomplete. When a premise is unused, the writer should either remove it or justify why it isn't needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of auxiliary constants / effective bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement asserts something 'eventually' or for 'sufficiently large' values, the proof should establish a specific value (e.g., an N that works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human solutions often give explicit bounds or a method to find them; omitting an explicit N when the problem calls for eventual behavior is a weakness. Example: the reviewer notes o3-mini-high failed to establish a specific N even though one should exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful asymptotic and coefficient accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymptotic claims must account for all contributing factors, including coefficients that can change growth order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: asserting an order-of-growth bound while ignoring that digit coefficients may themselves grow with n. Example from P1: the model's incorrect claim ignored the contribution from a_{k-1}, invalidating the claimed growth order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise verification and building toward generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: When generalizing, show base/small cases (e.g., i = k-2, k-3, ...) and use them to justify the general pattern rather than asserting 'and so on'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: work out several concrete small cases, detect the pattern, and then prove the general case. Anti-pattern: jumping immediately to the general claim without validating representative cases or giving a clear inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, insight, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer proofs that clearly expose the underlying idea and are concise; proofs that merely 'get to the finish line' without illuminating structure are weaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author compares the model's 'low road' solution (correct-but-slog) to Evan Chen's concise solution which gives clearer insight (e.g., remainder/division interpretation). A better-written proof often states the key idea up front and makes the structure evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and self-contained final proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and summarize all steps into a single, self-contained final proof that stands on its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than a sequence of partial chat responses, produce a single coherent proof that contains definitions, lemmas, and all justifications. This is what graders see; a scattered chain-of-thought is less useful for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding bluffing / verifiable steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Every assertion should be checkable; beware of confidently-phrased but unsupported claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models may 'sneak bullshit' past a reader; graders and authors should verify each step. Anti-patterns include bluffing completion, claiming results without proof, or relying on opaque heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative construction-finding for geometry / combinatorial problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that hinge on a key construction (e.g., choosing S = points outside the circle with diameter PQ, recognizing a Gabriel graph) require creativity to discover the construction and then prove its properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such problems, the crucial metric is whether the solution finds the right construction and then proves required properties (connectivity, planarity). The author found o3-mini-high required being given the construction to make progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving auxiliary lemmas and logical structure explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the argument into clear subclaims/lemmas (e.g., WLOG reductions, existence of consecutive zero coefficients, lemma that two consecutive zeros imply non-real-root property) and prove them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human solutions commonly proceed by a sequence of numbered logical steps; the model sometimes fails to supply one of these (e.g., step (1) in P2). Good proofs state and prove each auxiliary claim needed for the final contradiction or conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate WLOG reductions and problem simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Make standard WLOG assumptions and reductions (e.g., take k = n-1) where justified to simplify the problem without loss of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the WLOG step and justify it. Failure to consider or use natural reductions can block progress; giving the model helpful WLOG restatements sometimes enables correct subsequent reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling generality and edge cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure arguments are valid for the full stated domain (e.g., do not implicitly assume finiteness or other unstated restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: an argument that only works under an extra assumption (e.g., finite set of cities) when the problem allows infinite configurations. Always check domain-wide validity and address boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating how intermediate results imply the final property
rubrics_metrics.description: Show clearly how each proven intermediate fact (lemmas) leads to the desired final conclusion (connectivity, contradiction, no-all-real-roots, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in P2, after proving a lemma about consecutive zero coefficients, explicitly link it to the claim that a polynomial with all real nonzero roots cannot have such coefficients. Avoid leaving the reader to infer the logical bridge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task-format and training considerations for model-produced proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Models trained primarily on short-answer tasks may underperform on proof-writing; training methods (e.g., RL with binary reward, chain-of-thought length) affect ability to produce proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-guideline for producing/evaluating AI proofs: expect models optimized on short-form answers to need extra prompting or longer chain-of-thought to reach proof-level performance. Techniques like targeted RL on proof correctness or encouraging longer internal reasoning chains may improve results.
